findings.label: Regular Fused
findings.description: Fused construction bonds a synthetic interlining to the back of the outer fabric using heat and adhesive, creating immediate structure without any hand-stitching. The result is a jacket that feels uniform and stiff from the first wear, with flat lapels that lack the gentle roll of a canvassed garment. Over time — especially with dry-cleaning — the glue degrades and the interlining separates from the face cloth, causing the characteristic bubbling delamination that ruins a fused jacket irreparably.

findings.label: Ultra-thin Half Canvas
findings.description: Ultra-thin half canvas uses an exceptionally lightweight horsehair and linen canvas restricted to the chest and lapel zone, approaching the featherweight territory of Neapolitan unstructured tailoring while retaining a soft chest shape. The jacket drapes with a whisper of form, moving almost like a shirt on the body, making it ideal for tropical and super-lightweight fabrics where any additional mass would be suffocating. findings.label: Regular Half Canvas
findings.description: Standard half canvas is the workhorse of quality tailoring: a horsehair and linen canvas running from the shoulder seam down to roughly the mid-chest, hand-padstitched through the lapels to create their characteristic rolling break. Below the canvas, the lower body is stabilised with a light fused interlining, striking a practical balance between genuine craft and production economy. The result is a jacket that drapes naturally at the chest and lapel — where 80% of the visual impression is formed — and holds a crisper, more dimensional front than any fully fused garment.

findings.label: No Padding
findings.description: No padding produces the most natural, body-following shoulder possible — the sleeve is set into the armhole so the jacket falls directly from the wearer's natural shoulder point with no added projection or squaring. Associated above all with Neapolitan tailoring and the spalla camicia (shirt shoulder) tradition, this construction gives the jacket an almost relaxed, casually aristocratic quality: soft, human, and free of any militaristic squareness. It demands a clean natural shoulder from the wearer to look its best, but rewards one with a silhouette of exceptional ease and grace.

findings.label: Standard Machine
findings.description: A standard machine-made jacket relies entirely on industrial sewing machines for all seams, canvas attachment, and finishing, producing consistent and precise results at higher speed and lower cost than hand finishing. Long structural seams — back, side, sleeves — are done by machine in virtually all jackets including bespoke, as the straight length does not benefit from hand work. The overall character is uniform and neat, but lacks the subtle organic variation and flex of hand-sewn construction, and the jacket's canvas is typically fused or machine-padded rather than shaped by hand.

findings.label: Individual Handmade Parts
findings.description: A jacket with individual handmade parts combines machine sewing for long structural seams with hand work concentrated on the areas where it matters most: pad-stitching the lapels and collar canvas, hand-setting the sleeves into the armhole, hand-finishing the buttonholes, and hand-attaching the lining at its edges. This hybrid approach is the norm for the majority of high-quality bespoke and premium made-to-measure houses and delivers much of the softness, shape retention, and sartorial character of full handmade at a more practical time investment. It is the standard most discerning wearers associate with the term 'bespoke.'

findings.label: 0.15 cm by Hand
findings.description: Hand pick stitching at 0.15 cm is the most traditional and prized of all edge-finishing techniques: a tailor runs a needle through the underside of the facing and catches just a single thread on the surface at intervals of approximately 1.5 mm, producing a delicate broken line that no machine can truly replicate. The minute irregularities in spacing and thread tension that result from the human hand give the edge a living, textured quality that rewards close examination, and this is the definitive mark of a Savile Row or Neapolitan bespoke jacket. It takes considerable skill and time but results in an edge that is both perfectly sharp and softly organic.

findings.label: 0.6 cm by Hand
findings.description: A 0.6 cm hand pick stitch is set further from the edge and is individually pierced by hand, producing a clearly visible row of deliberate, evenly spaced surface stitches that form one of the most recognisable decorative signatures in high tailoring. Known as a 'swelled edge' in English tailoring tradition, this detail was a staple of Anthony Sinclair's work for Sean Connery's James Bond suits and is closely associated with the clean-cut English bespoke aesthetic. The slightly wider stitch distance makes each individual pick more visible and gives the lapel a bolder, more sporting character than the near-invisible 0.15 cm version.

findings.label: Full Lining
findings.description: A fully lined jacket has its entire interior — back, sides, front panels, and sleeves — covered with a smooth lining fabric, typically Bemberg cupro or silk, which makes the jacket slip effortlessly over a shirt, helps it retain its pressed shape, and finishes the interior to a uniform standard. Full lining is the default for formal suits, winter-weight cloths, and any jacket intended for frequent wear in professional settings, as it prolongs the life of the outer cloth by reducing friction. The lining also provides an opportunity to introduce colour, pattern, or a monogrammed label as a hidden personal statement.

findings.label: Half Lining
findings.description: A half-lined jacket retains lining on the front panels and the upper half of the back but leaves the lower back unlined, exposing the reverse of the fabric or a neat turned-and-stitched seam finish. This construction substantially reduces the jacket's weight and improves ventilation across the back — where body heat accumulates most — without sacrificing the easy-donning comfort of lined front panels. It is the preferred choice for medium-weight spring and autumn suits and for bespoke clients who want a single jacket to serve across a broad range of temperatures.

findings.label: Quarter Lining
findings.description: Quarter lining restricts lining coverage to only the top portion of the back and the sleeve tubes, leaving the lower back and the under-arms entirely unlined and finished in the cloth itself. This is the cooler, more Southern-Italian approach to lining, commonly specified for linen, cotton, and lightweight fresco summer jackets where maximum breathability is the priority. The exposed interior seams must be finished to a high standard — typically hand-felled — which paradoxically makes a quarter-lined jacket more demanding and expensive to produce than a fully lined one.

findings.label: Unlined
findings.description: An entirely unlined jacket is the ultimate expression of lightweight, warm-weather tailoring, with nothing between the outer cloth and the wearer's skin but the jacket's canvas and seam allowances, all of which must be finished to a standard fit for open inspection. The absence of lining allows the construction — canvassing, seam edges, inner pockets — to be seen and examined, demanding higher craftsmanship and making the garment breathe maximally. Unlined jackets hang with a particularly clean, soft drape because there is no lining resistance, and they are the preferred choice for resort, summer, and casual bespoke commissions.

findings.label: Matching to Fabric
findings.description: A matching lining is cut from a fabric whose tone, texture, or pattern coordinates closely with the outer cloth — for example, a grey flannel suit lined in a charcoal Bemberg cupro — so that when the jacket flares open in motion, the interior reads as a deliberate continuation rather than a contrasting surprise. This choice is typically favoured for conservative formal suiting where understatement is the brief, and it gives the jacket a unified, monolithic character that reads as sober and assured. The matching lining also tends to be the least distracting choice for fabrics with strong surface character such as windowpane check or pinstripe.

findings.label: Navy Solid
findings.description: A navy solid lining is among the most versatile and handsome interior choices across all suit colours — it pairs naturally with grey, charcoal, and brown outer fabrics while introducing a subtle nautical richness that reads confidently when the jacket lapels fall open. Navy Bemberg or silk lining gives the interior a clean, formal character that contrasts without clashing, making it a safe upgrade from a matching lining for anyone wanting a quiet personality note inside their suit. It is widely offered by English and Italian bespoke houses as the standard 'house lining' recommendation for business suiting.

findings.label: Black
findings.description: Black lining is the natural choice for formal evening wear — tuxedos, dinner suits, and black-tie jackets — where it creates a seamlessly dark interior that reinforces the jacket's dressiest register. Against lighter fabrics such as ivory or midnight blue it provides a crisp, high-contrast flash when the jacket moves, and for dark wool suits it produces a unified, solemn depth that suits both City formality and evening elegance. Black linings are also practical, as they are more resistant to visible soiling and fading than pale or patterned alternatives.

findings.label: Cream / Ivory
findings.description: A cream or ivory lining introduces warmth and a sense of historic luxury to the jacket interior, evoking the soft interiors of Edwardian dress coats and vintage English suiting from the golden age of bespoke tailoring. It is particularly effective in dark navy, charcoal, or black outer fabrics where the pale interior creates a luminous flash of contrast when the jacket opens, and it suits formal occasions where the wearer wants understated opulence rather than bold colour. Cream Bemberg or silk has a slightly warmer, more aged feeling than pure white and flatters virtually all skin tones when glimpsed at the lining edge.

findings.description: Dark charcoal lining occupies the tonal space between black and navy, offering a sober, serious interior that blends effortlessly with grey, charcoal, and dark blue outer fabrics without the stark formality of pure black. It is particularly popular in English business suiting where the overall look is one of controlled authority, and the near-neutral dark tone means the lining never distracts from the cloth's surface. Charcoal Bemberg cupro also ages gracefully without showing the yellowing or fading that lighter linings can develop over time.

findings.label: Regular Fused
findings.description: Fused construction bonds a synthetic interlining to the back of the outer fabric using heat and adhesive, creating immediate structure without any hand-stitching. The result is a jacket that feels uniform and stiff from the first wear, with flat lapels that lack the gentle roll of a canvassed garment. Over time — especially with dry-cleaning — the glue degrades and the interlining separates from the face cloth, causing the characteristic bubbling delamination that ruins a fused jacket irreparably.

findings.label: Ultra-thin Half Canvas
findings.description: Ultra-thin half canvas uses an exceptionally lightweight horsehair and linen canvas restricted to the chest and lapel zone, approaching the featherweight territory of Neapolitan unstructured tailoring while retaining a soft chest shape. The jacket drapes with a whisper of form, moving almost like a shirt on the body, making it ideal for tropical and super-lightweight fabrics where any additional mass would be suffocating. The chest maintains a subtle convex curve but the overall silhouette is deliberately understated and fluid.

findings.label: Regular Half Canvas
findings.description: Standard half canvas is the workhorse of quality tailoring: a horsehair and linen canvas running from the shoulder seam down to roughly the mid-chest, hand-padstitched through the lapels to create their characteristic rolling break. Below the canvas, the lower body is stabilised with a light fused interlining, striking a practical balance between genuine craft and production economy. The result is a jacket that drapes naturally at the chest and lapel — where 80% of the visual impression is formed — and holds a crisper, more dimensional front than any fully fused garment.

findings.label: No Padding
findings.description: No padding produces the most natural, body-following shoulder possible — the sleeve is set into the armhole so the jacket falls directly from the wearer's natural shoulder point with no added projection or squaring. Associated above all with Neapolitan tailoring and the spalla camicia (shirt shoulder) tradition, this construction gives the jacket an almost relaxed, casually aristocratic quality: soft, human, and free of any militaristic squareness. It demands a clean natural shoulder from the wearer to look its best, but rewards one with a silhouette of exceptional ease and grace.

findings.label: +0.1 cm (Both Sides)
findings.description: A 1mm padding addition is essentially imperceptible to the naked eye but just enough to square the shoulder point by a fraction and prevent any slight hollowing that occurs when a jacket hangs without support at the sleeve head. This is the most subtle intervention in the spectrum of shoulder construction — barely there, simply ensuring the garment has an impeccable, defined edge.

The buttonholes are almost always hand-worked in a gimp thread, producing a dense, slightly raised finish with subtle colour-matched or contrasting thread. This detail is impossible to add after the fact, confirming to any knowledgeable observer that the jacket was made from scratch to the wearer's precise measurements.

findings.label: No Vent
findings.description: A ventless back presents an unbroken, clean horizontal line across the entire hem of the jacket — no slits, no flaps, nothing to interrupt the silhouette from behind. Most closely associated with Italian tailoring and tuxedos globally, it creates a sleek, close-fitting appearance that flatters a slim physique and reads as fashion-forward and elegant when standing. The trade-off is mobility: sitting or reaching forward causes the back to pull and bunch, making it the least practical option for anyone who spends significant time seated.

findings.label: Side Vents
findings.description: Side vents — two symmetrical vertical slits at the rear side seams — are the hallmark of British tailoring and the most functionally satisfying of all vent options. They allow the jacket to open evenly on both sides when the wearer sits or reaches into trouser pockets, meaning the back drapes flat and uninterrupted whether standing or moving. The double vent is considered the most refined option in classic English dress, communicating an understanding of tailoring tradition without any overt showiness, and is the standard configuration on Savile Row bespoke.

A loose martingale is the more sporting, country-house variant of this detail, found on hacking jackets, tweed coats, and cavalry-inspired tailoring. findings.label: Standard Machine
findings.description: A standard machine-made jacket relies entirely on industrial sewing machines for all seams, canvas attachment, and finishing, producing consistent and precise results at higher speed and lower cost than hand finishing. Long structural seams — back, side, sleeves — are done by machine in virtually all jackets including bespoke, as the straight length does not benefit from hand work. The overall character is uniform and neat, but lacks the subtle organic variation and flex of hand-sewn construction, and the jacket's canvas is typically fused or machine-padded rather than shaped by hand.

findings.label: Individual Handmade Parts
findings.description: A jacket with individual handmade parts combines machine sewing for long structural seams with hand work concentrated on the areas where it matters most: pad-stitching the lapels and collar canvas, hand-setting the sleeves into the armhole, hand-finishing the buttonholes, and hand-attaching the lining at its edges. This hybrid approach is the norm for the majority of high-quality bespoke and premium made-to-measure houses and delivers much of the softness, shape retention, and sartorial character of full handmade at a more practical time investment. It is the standard most discerning wearers associate with the term 'bespoke.'

findings.label: 0.15 cm by Hand
findings.description: Hand pick stitching at 0.15 cm is the most traditional and prized of all edge-finishing techniques: a tailor runs a needle through the underside of the facing and catches just a single thread on the surface at intervals of approximately 1.5 mm, producing a delicate broken line that no machine can truly replicate. The minute irregularities in spacing and thread tension that result from the human hand give the edge a living, textured quality that rewards close examination, and this is the definitive mark of a Savile Row or Neapolitan bespoke jacket. It takes considerable skill and time but results in an edge that is both perfectly sharp and softly organic.

findings.label: 0.6 cm by Hand
findings.description: A 0.6 cm hand pick stitch is set further from the edge and is individually pierced by hand, producing a clearly visible row of deliberate, evenly spaced surface stitches that form one of the most recognisable decorative signatures in high tailoring. Known as a 'swelled edge' in English tailoring tradition, this detail was a staple of Anthony Sinclair's work for Sean Connery's James Bond suits and is closely associated with the clean-cut English bespoke aesthetic. The slightly wider stitch distance makes each individual pick more visible and gives the lapel a bolder, more sporting character than the near-invisible 0.15 cm version.

findings.label: Full Lining
findings.description: A fully lined jacket has its entire interior — back, sides, front panels, and sleeves — covered with a smooth lining fabric, typically Bemberg cupro or silk, which makes the jacket slip effortlessly over a shirt, helps it retain its pressed shape, and finishes the interior to a uniform standard. Full lining is the default for formal suits, winter-weight cloths, and any jacket intended for frequent wear in professional settings, as it prolongs the life of the outer cloth by reducing friction. The lining also provides an opportunity to introduce colour, pattern, or a monogrammed label as a hidden personal statement.

findings.label: Half Lining
findings.description: A half-lined jacket retains lining on the front panels and the upper half of the back but leaves the lower back unlined, exposing the reverse of the fabric or a neat turned-and-stitched seam finish. This construction substantially reduces the jacket's weight and improves ventilation across the back — where body heat accumulates most — without sacrificing the easy-donning comfort of lined front panels. It is the preferred choice for medium-weight spring and autumn suits and for bespoke clients who want a single jacket to serve across a broad range of temperatures.

findings.label: Quarter Lining
findings.description: Quarter lining restricts lining coverage to only the top portion of the back and the sleeve tubes, leaving the lower back and the under-arms entirely unlined and finished in the cloth itself. This is the cooler, more Southern-Italian approach to lining, commonly specified for linen, cotton, and lightweight fresco summer jackets where maximum breathability is the priority. The exposed interior seams must be finished to a high standard — typically hand-felled — which paradoxically makes a quarter-lined jacket more demanding and expensive to produce than a fully lined one.

findings.label: Unlined
findings.description: An entirely unlined jacket is the ultimate expression of lightweight, warm-weather tailoring, with nothing between the outer cloth and the wearer's skin but the jacket's canvas and seam allowances, all of which must be finished to a standard fit for open inspection. The absence of lining allows the construction — canvassing, seam edges, inner pockets — to be seen and examined, demanding higher craftsmanship and making the garment breathe maximally. Unlined jackets hang with a particularly clean, soft drape because there is no lining resistance, and they are the preferred choice for resort, summer, and casual bespoke commissions.

findings.label: Regular Fused
findings.description: Fused construction bonds a synthetic interlining to the back of the outer fabric using heat and adhesive, creating immediate structure without any hand-stitching. The result is a jacket that feels uniform and stiff from the first wear, with flat lapels that lack the gentle roll of a canvassed garment. Over time — especially with dry-cleaning — the glue degrades and the interlining separates from the face cloth, causing the characteristic bubbling delamination that ruins a fused jacket irreparably.

findings.label: Ultra-thin Half Canvas
findings.description: Ultra-thin half canvas uses an exceptionally lightweight horsehair and linen canvas restricted to the chest and lapel zone, approaching the featherweight territory of Neapolitan unstructured tailoring while retaining a soft chest shape. The jacket drapes with a whisper of form, moving almost like a shirt on the body, making it ideal for tropical and super-lightweight fabrics where any additional mass would be suffocating. The chest maintains a subtle convex curve but the overall silhouette is deliberately understated and fluid.

findings.description: Light half canvas uses a reduced-weight horsehair canvas from shoulder to mid-chest, offering noticeably more drape and softness than standard half canvas while still preserving a clean chest architecture and a lapel with genuine roll. The jacket breaks in gracefully and moulds gently to the torso over time without the full conforming memory of a true full-floating canvas.

findings.label: Regular Half Canvas
findings.description: Standard half canvas is the workhorse of quality tailoring: a horsehair and linen canvas running from the shoulder seam down to roughly the mid-chest, hand-padstitched through the lapels to create their characteristic rolling break. Below the canvas, the lower body is stabilised with a light fused interlining, striking a practical balance between genuine craft and production economy. The result is a jacket that drapes naturally at the chest and lapel — where 80% of the visual impression is formed — and holds a crisper, more dimensional front than any fully fused garment.

findings.label: No Padding
findings.description: No padding produces the most natural, body-following shoulder possible — the sleeve is set into the armhole so the jacket falls directly from the wearer's natural shoulder point with no added projection or squaring. Associated above all with Neapolitan tailoring and the spalla camicia (shirt shoulder) tradition, this construction gives the jacket an almost relaxed, casually aristocratic quality: soft, human, and free of any militaristic squareness. It demands a clean natural shoulder from the wearer to look its best, but rewards one with a silhouette of exceptional ease and grace.

findings.label: Standard Machine
findings.description: A standard machine-made jacket relies entirely on industrial sewing machines for all seams, canvas attachment, and finishing, producing consistent and precise results at higher speed and lower cost than hand finishing. Long structural seams — back, side, sleeves — are done by machine in virtually all jackets including bespoke, as the straight length does not benefit from hand work. The overall character is uniform and neat, but lacks the subtle organic variation and flex of hand-sewn construction, and the jacket's canvas is typically fused or machine-padded rather than shaped by hand.

findings.label: Individual Handmade Parts
findings.description: A jacket with individual handmade parts combines machine sewing for long structural seams with hand work concentrated on the areas where it matters most: pad-stitching the lapels and collar canvas, hand-setting the sleeves into the armhole, hand-finishing the buttonholes, and hand-attaching the lining at its edges. This hybrid approach is the norm for the majority of high-quality bespoke and premium made-to-measure houses and delivers much of the softness, shape retention, and sartorial character of full handmade at a more practical time investment. It is the standard most discerning wearers associate with the term 'bespoke.'

The minute irregularities in spacing and thread tension that result from the human hand give the edge a living, textured quality that rewards close examination, and this is the definitive mark of a Savile Row or Neapolitan bespoke jacket. findings.label: Full Lining
findings.description: A fully lined jacket has its entire interior — back, sides, front panels, and sleeves — covered with a smooth lining fabric, typically Bemberg cupro or silk, which makes the jacket slip effortlessly over a shirt, helps it retain its pressed shape, and finishes the interior to a uniform standard. Full lining is the default for formal suits, winter-weight cloths, and any jacket intended for frequent wear in professional settings, as it prolongs the life of the outer cloth by reducing friction. The lining also provides an opportunity to introduce colour, pattern, or a monogrammed label as a hidden personal statement.

findings.label: Half Lining
findings.description: A half-lined jacket retains lining on the front panels and the upper half of the back but leaves the lower back unlined, exposing the reverse of the fabric or a neat turned-and-stitched seam finish. This construction substantially reduces the jacket's weight and improves ventilation across the back — where body heat accumulates most — without sacrificing the easy-donning comfort of lined front panels. It is the preferred choice for medium-weight spring and autumn suits and for bespoke clients who want a single jacket to serve across a broad range of temperatures.

findings.label: Quarter Lining
findings.description: Quarter lining restricts lining coverage to only the top portion of the back and the sleeve tubes, leaving the lower back and the under-arms entirely unlined and finished in the cloth itself. This is the cooler, more Southern-Italian approach to lining, commonly specified for linen, cotton, and lightweight fresco summer jackets where maximum breathability is the priority. The exposed interior seams must be finished to a high standard — typically hand-felled — which paradoxically makes a quarter-lined jacket more demanding and expensive to produce than a fully lined one.

findings.label: Unlined
findings.description: An entirely unlined jacket is the ultimate expression of lightweight, warm-weather tailoring, with nothing between the outer cloth and the wearer's skin but the jacket's canvas and seam allowances, all of which must be finished to a standard fit for open inspection. The absence of lining allows the construction — canvassing, seam edges, inner pockets — to be seen and examined, demanding higher craftsmanship and making the garment breathe maximally. Unlined jackets hang with a particularly clean, soft drape because there is no lining resistance, and they are the preferred choice for resort, summer, and casual bespoke commissions.
